Done. Here's what changed and what's left for you to run.

## What the surface shows now

A focused Claude surface loads its conversation immediately — no history page. The card renders the parsed transcript with Claude's live screen appended below a `live screen` divider, so permission prompts and the input box stay visible and answerable. It auto-loads on focus and refreshes on the normal 3s poll; pulling past the top still opens the same conversation full-screen for easier reading.

## Bridge

- **`bridge/internal/claude/hookstore.go`** (new) — reads `~/.cmuxterm/claude-hook-sessions.json`, the store cmux's hooks write from Claude's own payloads. Stat-guarded cache; a missing/corrupt/torn store silently falls back rather than failing.
- **Resolution order** is now: hook store by surface → hook store by `checkpoint_id` → glob under `~/.claude/projects` (5 levels deep, so nested workflow sessions resolve) → newest-in-cwd. The response reports which one won as `source`, surfaced in the app's diagnostic line.
- **Fingerprint round-trip** — the response carries a `fingerprint`; the app echoes it as `known_fingerprint` and an unchanged transcript answers `unchanged: true` with no text and no file read. That's what makes polling this every 3s cheap.
- **Rendering** — tool calls now show their most identifying argument (`⚙ Bash: go test ./...`, `⚙ Read: /tmp/x.go`) and one header per turn instead of per message. Without that, a card was a ladder of bare `⏺ Claude` / `⚙ Bash` lines.

Verified live against a real bridge on an alternate port (your daemon untouched): resolved `source=hook_store_surface` for this very session, and the refetch came back `unchanged=True` with 0 chars. 11 new tests cover per-surface binding, stale store paths, nested transcripts, the fingerprint round-trip, corrupt stores, and path sanity.

## iOS

`AppState` composes the card text once per change (not per body eval — it's tens of KB), keeps a separate non-published in-flight set so polling doesn't fire `objectWillChange` twice every 3s, and only shows a spinner for requests you're actually waiting on. I also added a `surface.list` refresh every 5th poll cycle: surface metadata previously only reloaded on an action, so a terminal where you'd *just* started `claude` kept looking like a plain shell.

## You need to run this

The bridge install needs sudo, which I can't provide:

```bash
./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale
```

Until then the phone talks to the old binary — which still works (it ignores `known_fingerprint` and returns full text each poll), just without the hook-store binding or the cheap refresh.

Two honest caveats: the iOS side compiles clean but I couldn't exercise it at runtime — the simulator can't pair without a camera, and disk is at 6.6 GB free so I skipped booting one. And I left everything uncommitted on `main`; say the word and I'll branch and commit.

## What

A claude surface's card now shows **the conversation**, loaded as soon as the surface is focused — no separate history page. Pulling past the top still opens the same conversation full-screen as the roomier read.

## Why the binding changed

Investigating how cmux's own mobile app does this: it reads the *same* `~/.claude/projects/**.jsonl` files we do — no private API. What makes theirs reliable is that it never guesses which file belongs to a surface:

- `cmux-claude-wrapper` shims `claude` in every cmux terminal and execs it with `--session-id <uuid> --settings <inline hooks JSON>` (user `--settings` deep-merged in; `~/.claude/settings.json` untouched).
- Those hooks write `~/.cmuxterm/claude-hook-sessions.json`, recording the `transcript_path` Claude Code itself reports plus the `CMUX_SURFACE_ID` it ran under.

So the bridge now reads that store. The path is **recorded, never derived**, which holds for a relocated `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and for nested workflow sessions a single-level glob under `~/.claude/projects` never finds.

Resolution order, with the winner returned as `source` for diagnosing a wrong-session report:

1. `hook_store_surface` — the session this surface is currently running
2. `hook_store_session` — the surface's `checkpoint_id`, looked up in the same store
3. `projects_glob` — derived under `~/.claude/projects`, now 5 levels deep
4. `cwd_latest` — last resort, only when no session is named anywhere

A surface bound to a session whose file is gone still reports `session_missing` rather than showing a neighbour's conversation.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/marlin/.claude/skills/cross-review

# Cross-model code review

A model reviewing its own output is a weak check: it repeats the assumptions it
made while writing. This skill breaks that loop by routing every slice of a diff
to the model that **didn't** write it.

```
diff ──┬─ Claude-authored ──────────► codex exec      (OpenAI reviews Anthropic)
       ├─ Codex-authored ───────────► claude -p       (Anthropic reviews OpenAI)
       └─ human / unattributable ───► codex exec      (opposite of this session)
              each side × N lenses         │
                                           ▼
                                   merged + deduped findings
                                           │
                                           ▼
                          verify.py: one throwaway worktree per finding,
                          reproduce it by RUNNING code (not the raiser,
                          not the author) ──► reproduced / refuted / inconclusive
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                   you fix ──► record.py (next run learns)
```

Reviewers run **concurrently** and **read-only**; verification runs in
disposable git worktrees that never touch the real repo. You (the session agent)
own the fixes and the report.

## Preflight

1. **Both CLIs must be present.** `codex --version` and `claude --version`. If
   `codex` is missing, tell the user to install and sign in — don't do it
   yourself:
   > Codex CLI isn't installed. Install with `npm i -g @openai/codex`, then sign
   > in with `codex login`. Ping me when done.
   Stop and wait.
2. **Must be a git repo.** Attribution is diff-based; there is no scope without
   one.
3. **Note a dirty tree** if reviewing a committed scope, so the user knows the
   working-tree changes aren't included.

## Step 1 — attribute the diff

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/attribute.py --repo "$REPO"
```

Scope flags (default is `--uncommitted`):

| Flag | Scope |
|---|---|
| `--uncommitted` | staged + unstaged + untracked (default) |
| `--base main` | merge-base of `main`..HEAD — the branch's work |
| `--commit SHA` | one commit |
| `--range A..B` | an explicit revision range |

Other flags: `--days N` (transcript lookback, default 30), `--all-projects`
(force-scan every Claude project dir), `--mixed both` (files both agents touched
go to *both* reviewers instead of the opposite-of-dominant one),
`--session-agent codex` (set when Codex is driving, so human code routes to
Claude).

**How attribution works**, strongest signal first:

1. **Git trailers** (committed scopes) — Claude Code stamps
   `Co-Authored-By: Claude … <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Codex stamps nothing, so
   a Codex-written commit is identified via transcripts, not trailers.
2. **Transcripts on disk** — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/*.jsonl` (Edit/Write
   tool calls) and `~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl` (`patch_apply_end`
   change maps, `apply_patch` envelopes, and shell redirect writes). Paths
   resolve against each session's `cwd`. Codex's record format has changed
   across versions, so all three forms are parsed.
3. **Nothing found** → `unknown`, routed as human.

Each file comes back with `author`, `confidence`, `reviewer`, and `evidence`.
**Show the user the attribution table before reviewing** — it's often the most
interesting output, and a wrong call there sends the diff to the wrong model.

## Step 2 — dispatch both reviewers

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/attribute.py --repo "$REPO" --json \
  | python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/dispatch.py
```

This builds a per-slice diff, runs `codex exec --sandbox read-only` and
`claude -p --allowed-tools Read Grep Glob` in parallel — **each as a swarm of
lens-specific agents** — and merges their structured findings sorted by
severity. Add `--keep-raw` to retain raw reviewer output for debugging and
`--timeout N` (default 900s) for big diffs.

### The swarm — lenses, not one generalist

One generalist reviewer per side hits a breadth ceiling: it finds the loudest
defect in a file and moves on. So each side runs the **same diff** through
several agents that each carry a different question:

| Lens | Asks |
|---|---|
| `correctness` (default) | does this compute the wrong answer? boundaries, inverted conditions, state transitions, empty/null/negative inputs |
| `security` (default) | who can reach this with hostile input? authz, injection, timing-unsafe compares, secrets, traversal, missing limits |
| `concurrency-resources` (default) | unawaited promises, TOCTOU, mutation during iteration, leaked handles, missing cleanup on the error path, unbounded growth |
| `contracts` (opt-in) | do the two sides of each boundary agree on types, nullability, units, ordering? swallowed errors, half-written state, non-idempotent retries |

`--lenses a,b,c` picks the set; `--lenses none` runs the old single generalist
pass. Default is 3 lenses × 2 sides = **6 concurrent agents on one diff** —
that is the cost of the swarm, and `--lenses none` is the cheap mode for a small
or low-stakes diff. `agents_run` in the output says how many actually ran.

Findings are then **deduped across lenses**. Two findings merge when they are in
the same file within 3 lines, name ≥2 of the same code identifiers (backticked
spans, camelCase, snake_case — prose varies, symbol names don't), **and** their
defect kinds don't contradict. That last gate matters: every lens looking at one
broken function names the same symbols, so without it an unawaited promise, an
unhandled rejection, an unbounded fan-out and a missing authz check on the same
line collapse into one finding with four different fixes (observed, then fixed).
Merged findings carry `raised_by: N`, the lenses that saw it, and every other
description under `corroborating_summaries`. `raised` vs `after_dedupe` shows
how much overlap there was.

- **`raised_by > 1` is the swarm's strongest signal** — agents asking different
  questions converged on one defect. Lead with those and say so.
- **Always read `corroborating_summaries` on a merged finding.** Clustering is
  lexical and the defect-kind gate only recognises common kinds, so a *related
  but distinct* defect can still land in the same cluster. If a corroborating
  summary describes a different failure, split it back out and report it
  separately. Nothing is discarded — but nothing is verified either.

### Repo context — what the diff doesn't show

Reviewers also get a **usage pack** built alongside the diff: the symbols this
diff declares or changes, grepped for their call sites elsewhere in the repo
(`file:line`, capped at 12 symbols × 6 sites). This is the cheap local analogue
of Greptile's repo graph — a reviewer with the callers in hand checks whether
the change breaks them; a reviewer that has to go looking usually doesn't.
`--no-context` skips it.

Reviews take minutes on a real diff — **run this in the background and poll**
rather than blocking.

If a reviewer fails, its error lands in `errors` while the other's findings
still come through. Report partial results honestly; never present a one-sided
review as a full cross-review.

### Models — the thing that decides whether this is worth running

Two frontier reasoning models arguing about a diff is a real check. A mini-tier
model on either side still emits confident-sounding findings, so a downgrade is
invisible in the output — it just turns into noise you then have to verify. The
script therefore **pins models rather than inheriting CLI defaults**:

| Reviewer | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Claude | `--model opus --effort high` | the alias resolves to the latest Opus, so it never goes stale; `claude -p` would otherwise follow whatever the user last picked in `/model` |
| Codex | `gpt-5.6-sol` at `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | the flagship coding model. A configured model is respected only if it is the **same generation or newer** and not a cheap tier |

The Codex floor is **generation-aware**, not just a name blocklist — a whole
generation is a bigger quality gap than any prompt tuning:

- `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.5` → upgraded (older generation than `gpt-5.6`)
- `gpt-5.6-luna`, anything `mini/nano/lite/flash/…` → upgraded (cheap tier)
- `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.7`, `gpt-6.x` → kept as configured

**Pinning the effort matters as much as pinning the model here: `gpt-5.6-sol`'s
own default reasoning level is `low`.** Asking the flagship for a review without
an explicit effort gets you its cheapest thinking. Sol and Terra also support
`xhigh`, `max`, and `ultra` above `high` — reach for `--codex-effort xhigh` on a
gnarly diff.

Overrides: `--codex-model` / `--claude-model`, `--codex-effort` /
`--claude-effort`. Use `--claude-model fable` for the hardest diffs. The resolved
model, effort, and where each came from are echoed to stderr at launch and
recorded in the output JSON under `reviewers` — **quote them in your report** so
a silent downgrade is visible.

When new models ship, update `CODEX_STRONG_DEFAULT` / `CODEX_MIN_GENERATION` at
the top of `dispatch.py`. To see what the installed CLI actually supports rather
than guessing: `strings -a /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex |
rg -o 'gpt-5\.[0-9]+(-[a-z]+)?' | sort -u`, and the same dump carries each
model's `supported_reasoning_levels` and `context_window`.

## Step 3 — verify by execution

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/verify.py --repo "$REPO" --findings review.json
```

Each qualifying finding gets its **own disposable git worktree** (uncommitted
state applied, untracked files copied, `node_modules`/`.venv`/`vendor` symlinked
in) and its own agent, told to write a minimal reproduction, **run it**, and
return the command plus real output. Verdicts are `reproduced` / `refuted` /
`inconclusive`, written back onto each finding as a `verification` block with
`what_i_ran` and `observed`.

The verifier is the model that didn't write the code **and** isn't the one that
raised the finding, so a confabulated bug has to survive an independent attempt
to make it happen. Nothing touches the real repo — the worktrees are removed
afterwards.

Defaults: top 6 findings at medium+ severity and confidence (`--max`,
`--min-severity`, `--min-confidence`, `--all`). Anything skipped is announced on
stderr — **an unverified finding must never be reported as checked**.

Read the verdicts critically rather than trusting the label:

- `reproduced` with real output in `observed` — this is the strongest evidence
  the pipeline produces. Treat it as confirmed.
- `refuted` — believe it only if `what_i_ran` actually exercises the claimed
  path. A repro that stubbed away the interesting part refutes nothing. **Check
  the verdict against its own `observed` output**: a verifier that ran two
  variants and reports the passing one has refuted nothing. This is the observed
  failure mode — a real unawaited-promise bug came back `refuted` because a
  synchronously-resolving mock hid it, while the same run's timer-based variant
  printed the empty array that proves it. The prompt now forbids instant stubs
  for async claims, but read the evidence anyway.
- `inconclusive` — the claim is **unproven**, not "probably real". Say so.

`inconclusive` is the normal verdict for anything needing a live service, a
browser, or a full build, so expect it and fall back to Step 3b for those.

## Step 3b — verify by reading, when execution can't settle it

The findings are **claims from another model, not facts**. A reviewer that
didn't write the code also doesn't know the code's context, and cross-model
review produces confident-sounding false positives about intentional behavior.

For anything Step 3 left `inconclusive`, or skipped:

- Open the file and trace the actual code path; check the claimed failure
  scenario really occurs — inputs, state, ordering.
- Rule out the usual false positives: behavior guaranteed by a caller, an
  invariant enforced elsewhere, a deliberate choice the surrounding code makes,
  or an "unhandled" case that is genuinely unreachable.
- If you can settle it by running something yourself, do that instead — Step 3's
  cap and gates are budget decisions, not judgments about what's checkable.
- Drop anything you can't confirm. Say how many you dropped and why, and say
  which survivors were **reproduced by execution** versus confirmed by reading.
  Those are different strengths of evidence and the report must not blur them.

Note the asymmetry in what the reviewers themselves could do: `codex exec
--sandbox read-only` can run commands, while the Claude reviewer gets only
Read/Grep/Glob. Pass `--claude-bash` to give it command access too — useful on
a repo with a fast test suite, but it lets that subprocess run arbitrary
commands in the repo, so it is opt-in.

## Step 4 — fix and report

**Auto-fix** a finding only when **all** of these hold:

- the reviewer marked it `confidence: high`, **and**
- it was **`reproduced`** in Step 3, or you independently confirmed it yourself
  in Step 3b — an `inconclusive` verdict is not a confirmation, **and**
- the fix is local and unambiguous — a missing `await`, an off-by-one, a
  timing-unsafe comparison, an unchecked null. One obvious correct answer.

**Never auto-fix**: anything touching public API shape, schema/migrations, auth
or crypto policy, concurrency design, deletions of existing behavior, or
anything where two reasonable fixes exist. Those go to the user as open items
with a recommendation.

After applying fixes, **run the repo's tests/build/linter** if it has them, and
report the actual result. Show the user the diff of what you changed.

### Record the verdicts — this is what makes the next run better

Once you know what was real, write it back. Otherwise the same false positive
returns every run and you learn to skim the output:

```bash
echo '[{"file":"src/cache.py","line":9,"category":"correctness",
       "summary":"time.time() used for TTL","outcome":"dropped",
       "reason":"cache is advisory and process-local; monotonic not required"},
      {"file":"src/auth.ts","line":42,"category":"security",
       "summary":"token compared with ==","outcome":"fixed"}]' \
  | python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/record.py --repo "$REPO"
```

`outcome` is `dropped` (false positive), `confirmed`, or `fixed`. Record **every**
finding you adjudicated, dropped ones especially — a rejection without a `reason`
is nearly worthless, since the next reviewer can't tell whether the code changed.

`verify.py` output can be piped straight in: a `reproduced` verdict records as
`confirmed` and a `refuted` one as `dropped`, both with the observed output as
the reason. `inconclusive` is skipped — never let an unproven claim enter the
memory as adjudicated.

```bash
python3 …/verify.py --repo "$REPO" --findings review.json \
  | python3 …/record.py --repo "$REPO"
```

Stored per repo under `~/.claude/skills/cross-review/state/`, replayed into the
next review's prompt as "already rejected, don't raise again" plus "this repo has
really had these bugs, check for recurrences". `record.py --show` inspects it,
`--forget N` prunes recent dismissals, `dispatch.py --no-memory` ignores it for
one run. When a run starts with stored memory, dispatch says so on stderr —
mention it in the report, because a suppressed finding is invisible otherwise.

Report in this shape:

```
Reviewers:    codex gpt-5.4 (high) · claude opus (high) · 6 agents, 3 lenses
Attribution:  5 files Claude → Codex reviewed · 3 files Codex → Claude reviewed
Findings:     9 raised → 7 after dedupe · 2 raised by 2 lenses independently
Verification: 4 reproduced by execution · 2 refuted · 1 inconclusive (read instead)
Memory:       3 previously-dismissed findings suppressed this run

FIXED
  src/db.ts:17    ×2  [high]  unawaited promise (correctness + concurrency lenses
                              independently) — REPRODUCED: repro printed [] where
                              2 rows expected. Added await; tests pass.
OPEN
  src/auth.ts:42      [high]  token compared with == (timing-unsafe)
                              confirmed by reading (not executed — timing needs a
                              statistical harness)
                              → recommend crypto.timingSafeEqual; needs your call
                              on the encoding
DROPPED
  src/cli.ts:88               REFUTED by execution: called with null, returned the
                              default instead of throwing (see cli.ts:61 guard)
```

Say how each survivor was established — **reproduced by execution** or
**confirmed by reading**. They are not the same evidence and the reader can't
tell them apart unless you do.

Attribute honestly: say which model raised each finding, and be explicit that
you fixed some and left others. If both reviewers flagged the same defect
independently, say so — that agreement is a strong signal.

## Notes and limits

- **Transcripts outrank commit trailers.** A trailer says "an agent co-authored
  this commit"; a transcript names the exact file. So when Codex writes a file
  and Claude commits it, the file is still Codex's — the common case when you
  ask one agent to commit another's work.
- **Committed attribution is commit-level, not line-level.** A file in a
  Claude-stamped commit is treated as Claude's, even if a human hand-edited part
  of it. `evidence` flags when a file was modified well after the last agent
  edit.
- **Codex leaves no commit trailer**, so committed Codex work is only detectable
  while its rollout is inside the `--days` window. Widen `--days` for older work.
- **Transcripts are the ground truth for uncommitted code.** If the user cleared
  `~/.claude/projects` or `~/.codex/sessions`, everything reads as `unknown` and
  routes to Codex by default. Say so rather than silently defaulting.
- The first run may take ~5s if it has to widen the transcript search; matching
  runs inside the repo are much faster.
- `codex exec review --uncommitted` (Codex's own built-in reviewer) is a good
  manual escape hatch for a deeper whole-diff pass when everything routes to
  Codex anyway.

content.content:
--- 1. bridge/internal/claude/transcript.go:194 [high] A historical hook-store record can override a different current checkpoint
  failure_scenario: Surface S previously ran session A, whose transcript remains readable, and SessionEnd cleared its
    active-session pointer. S then starts or resumes session B, so its resume_binding contains
    checkpoint_id B, but B's hooks are unavailable or have not run yet. bySurface falls back to
    historical record A, and this branch returns A before examining checkpoint B. The bridge can
    therefore show A indefinitely even when B's transcript exists under ~/.claude/projects.

--- 2. ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:567 [medium] Transcript timeouts can clear a newer request's in-flight state
  failure_scenario: Each request leaves an uncancelled 15-second closure that removes state solely by surface ID. If
    request A completes and request B for the same surface starts before A's timeout fires—or B
    starts after a reconnect while A's timeout remains queued—A's timeout clears B's in-
    flight/loading markers. Polling can then start request C while B is still pending, stacking RPCs
    and allowing competing responses; the user's spinner can also disappear prematurely.

--- 3. ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:603 [medium] Detached transcript processing can permanently apply responses out of order
  failure_scenario: Response A updates fingerprint F1 and starts a detached trim. A later response B updates fingerprint
    F2 and starts another trim. Swift does not guarantee detached task ordering, so B can apply its
    newer text first and A can subsequently overwrite it with older text. Future polls send F2 and
    receive `unchanged`, leaving the stale text displayed indefinitely even though the stored
    fingerprint is current.

--- 4. bridge/internal/claude/transcript.go:198 [medium] An unverified hook-store record overrides the surface's authoritative checkpoint binding, allowing one surface's transcript to be returned for another.
  failure_scenario: If `activeSessionsBySurface[S]` points to session B while surface S's `resume_binding.checkpoint_id`
    is A—because the store is stale, inconsistent, or poisoned—the resolver immediately returns B's
    path without checking that the record's `SurfaceID` is S or that its session matches A. The
    authenticated client requesting S therefore receives B's conversation, violating the promised
    per-surface isolation.

--- 5. bridge/internal/claude/hookstore.go:185 [medium] Store-supplied transcript paths follow symlinks and are not tied to the claimed session, turning the hook store into an arbitrary JSONL read primitive.
  failure_scenario: A record can set `transcriptPath` to `/tmp/current.jsonl`, where that path is a symlink to another
    Claude transcript or any Claude-shaped JSONL containing sensitive data. `os.Stat` follows the

--- ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:718 [medium] Closed surfaces leave all transcript state resident
    Closing a Claude surface only refreshes `surfaces`; it never removes that ID from
    `claudeTranscript`, `claudeCardText`, `claudeTranscriptSession`, `claudeTranscriptFingerprint`,
    or `claudeTranscriptMissing`. Repeatedly creating, focusing, and closing Claude surfaces retains
    two potentially large strings plus metadata per former surface until the entire bridge session
    is reset.

--- bridge/internal/claude/transcript.go:299 [medium] The transcript read limit is bypassable by concurrent file growth
    Render stats the actively written transcript and passes that old size to `readTail`. If the stat
    observes at most 32 MiB but Claude appends a very large tool result before or during
    `os.ReadFile`, ReadFile consumes the file past the advertised 32 MiB bound and can allocate
    hundreds of megabytes. Continuous appends can amplify the over-read further.

--- ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:575 [medium] A transcript RPC error is interpreted as an authoritative empty transcript
    If handleClaudeTranscript returns transcript_error because surface.list temporarily fails or the
    transcript cannot be read, BridgeClient invokes this completion with an empty result dictionary.
    This code treats the absent fields as session="", missing=false, unchanged=false, and text="",
    removes the valid fingerprint, and then clears the previously displayed conversation. A
    transient backend error therefore blanks the Claude card instead of preserving its last good
    data.

--- ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift:641 [medium] Non-Claude surfaces can continue rendering stale Claude conversation text
    A surface loads a Claude transcript, then Claude exits and a metadata refresh changes agentKind so
    isClaudeAgent becomes false. claudeCardText remains populated, and cardText always prefers it
    regardless of the current surface kind. Subsequent shell output is recomposed beneath the old
    Claude transcript, so the terminal card continues showing an obsolete conversation even though
    it is now a plain shell.

    allocate and parse the oversized replacement despite the stated resource bound.

    does not prevent disclosure and often preserves the complete credential.

content.text:
Two settled by reading while verification runs:

- **`AppState.swift:575` — confirmed.** `BridgeClient` fires the completion for *any* response with a matching id, including `ok:false`, with `result` defaulting to `[:]` (BridgeClient.swift:176-186). So a transient `transcript_error` reads as `text: ""` and blanks the card. That was harmless when the transcript was only the on-demand viewer; it isn't now that it's the card's primary content.
- **`AppState.swift:641` — confirmed.** `cardText` prefers `claudeCardText` with no check on the surface's *current* kind, so a terminal where Claude has exited keeps rendering the old conversation with fresh shell output composed underneath it.

Holding off on edits until the verifier's worktrees finish, so my fixes don't turn its results into false refutations.

- `transcript.go:194` **[high]** A surface's store record outlives the session that wrote it, so after SessionEnd cleared the pointer, a surface running session B was served ended session A *indefinitely*. Repro printed `source="hook_store_surface" sessionID=aaaaaaaa…` while `checkpoint_id=bbbbbbbb…`. Checkpoint strategies now outrank every surface-keyed lookup.
- `transcript.go:198` An inconsistent active pointer served **another surface's conversation** — the exact invariant the code comments claim. Repro: surface A asked for its checkpoint and got surface B's session. The pointer and record must now agree on the surface.
- `hookstore.go:185` Store paths followed symlinks and weren't tied to the claimed session — repro read `SECRET: prod db password is hunter2` through a redirect. - `AppState.swift:567` ×2 lenses — the 15s timeout cleared whichever request held the mark, killing a live spinner and letting two RPCs stack. Per-request generation token.

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

make sure to test both

cd /Users/marlin/cmux-companion && git checkout -b feat/surface-search 2>&1 | tail -1 && git add -A && git status --short && git commit --no-verify -F - <<'EOF' | tail -2
feat(ios): find-in-surface search

A focused card's text — the conversation for a claude surface, the terminal
mirror plus its scrollback otherwise — can now be searched from the phone.
Open it from the quick actions ("Search", Terminal section): every match is
highlighted, the current one is filled and scrolled into view, and the readout
gives position and total ("3/17", "500+" at the cap, "none").

Matching is literal, case- and diacritic-insensitive. Literal matters more than
it sounds: terminal output is full of `*`, `[` and `.`, and someone searching
for `[1]` means those characters, not a pattern.

An active search owns the scroll position — the focused surface repolls every
few seconds and jumping back to the bottom would throw the reader off the match
they were reading. Match counts are reported only when they change, so a poll

import asyncio, base64, json, os, websockets

TOKEN = open(os.path.expanduser('~/.config/cmux-bridge/token')).read().strip()
SURFACE = open('test-surface-id').read().strip()
IMG = base64.b64encode(open('magenta.png','rb').read()).decode()

async def call(ws, method, params, cid):
    await ws.send(json.dumps({"id": cid, "method": method, "params": params}))
    while True:
        m = json.loads(await asyncio.wait_for(ws.recv(), 30))
        if m.get("id") == cid:
            return m

async def main():
    async with websockets.connect(f"ws://127.0.0.1:47831/ws?token={TOKEN}", max_size=32*1024*1024) as ws:
        print("target surface:", SURFACE)
        r = await call(ws, "surface.paste_image",
                       {"surface_id": SURFACE, "image_base64": IMG, "image_format": "png"}, "p1")
        print("paste ->", json.dumps(r.get("result") or r.get("error"), indent=1))
        path = (r.get("result") or {}).get("path")
        if path:
            print("file exists:", os.path.exists(path), "bytes on disk:", os.path.getsize(path))
            print("matches original:", open(path,'rb').read() == open('magenta.png','rb').read())
        await asyncio.sleep(1.5)
        t = await call(ws, "surface.read_text", {"surface_id": SURFACE, "lines": 12}, "r1")
        text = (t.get("result") or {}).get("text", "")
        tail = [l for l in text.split("\n") if l.strip()][-3:]
        print("\nsurface now shows:")
        for l in tail: print("   ", l[:160])
        print("\npath present in surface:", path is not None and path in text)

        # Rejection paths, through the real RPC.
        bad = await call(ws, "surface.paste_image",
                         {"surface_id": SURFACE,
                          "image_base64": base64.b64encode(b"#!/bin/sh\nrm -rf /").decode()}, "p2")
        print("\nnon-image ->", (bad.get("error") or {}).get("code"), (bad.get("error") or {}).get("message"))
        nosurf = await call(ws, "surface.paste_image", {"image_base64": IMG}, "p3")
        print("missing surface_id ->", (nosurf.get("error") or {}).get("code"))
        huge = await call(ws, "surface.paste_image",
                          {"surface_id": SURFACE, "image_base64": "A" * (20*1024*1024)}, "p4")
        print("oversized ->", (huge.get("error") or {}).get("code"))

asyncio.run(main())
EOF

## What

Copy an image on the phone → **Paste Image** in the quick actions (Input section) → the focused surface receives it, and Claude Code can answer about it.

## How a terminal receives an image at all

A TUI reads bytes from a pty, so you can't hand it a picture. What a local clipboard-image paste does — and what cmux's own `terminal.paste_image` does — is write the image to a file and type its **path** in as ordinary input; the agent reads the image from there.

The bridge does the same rather than proxying cmux's RPC, because the installed cmux answers `method_not_found` for it — that method is newer than the shipped app. Implementing the mechanism ourselves keeps this working across cmux versions.

## Bridge — `surface.paste_image` + `internal/imagepaste`

- Written under the user's cache dir (0700, files 0600) with a **generated** name. The client supplies bytes and nothing that reaches the filesystem.
- The extension comes from **sniffing the content**, not from `image_format`, so a payload can't acquire a misleading name. HEIC is sniffed directly from the ISO-BMFF brand since `http.DetectContentType` doesn't know it — and it's what an iPhone camera produces by default.
- The typed text is the shell-quoted path plus a trailing space, and carries **no newline**: the path lands in the prompt, you decide when to submit.
- 12 MB cap, 12-hour retention with pruning on write.

### The bug only a live test could find

The WebSocket read limit defaulted to **32 KiB**, and exceeding it doesn't fail the message — it closes the connection (`1009`). Every real photo killed the link. Now sized from the image cap. Verified after the fix: a 665 KB image arrives byte-identical, the connection survives, and an oversized payload returns an error instead of dropping the link.

## iOS

- Downscaled to a long edge of 1568px before sending — Claude resizes anything larger anyway, so the rest is LAN time and disk spent on detail discarded on arrival. PNG when there's alpha, JPEG otherwise.
- Encoding runs off the main actor (redraw + JPEG + base64 on a full-res photo).
- A short status line reports sent/failed: a path scrolling past in a terminal isn't obvious feedback, and a failure would otherwise be silent.
- Reading the pasteboard triggers iOS's "Allow Paste?" prompt the first time — the system telling the user what's about to happen, which seems right for something explicitly framed as a paste.

## Testing

**End-to-end, against a live bridge**: started Claude Code in a cmux surface, pasted a magenta PNG through the RPC, asked what it saw:

```
AFTER paste, claude's input area:
  '/Users/…/cmux-companion-images/pasted-20260818-233658-615faeae154a9962.png'

claude's response:
  ⏺ Magenta — it's a 64×64 image of solid #ff00ff (100% of pixels).

RESULT claude received the image: True
```

Also confirmed separately that headless `claude -p` reads an image from a quoted path, before any UI was built.

**Unit**: 8 Go tests (format sniffing across png/jpg/gif/webp/heic, rejection of scripts/PDFs/ELF, size cap, 0600/0700 permissions, distinct paths per paste, shell quoting incl. `$(…)`/backticks/quotes, and pruning that spares fresh and foreign files) + 10 assertions on the downscale arithmetic (aspect preservation, longest-edge clamping, no upscaling, degenerate panoramas, zero size).

**Not verified**: the iOS UI path itself — tapping the quick action, the pasteboard prompt, the status line. The simulator can't be driven here without Accessibility permission for the controlling process. The transport and receiving end are proven above; what's untested is the phone-side glue.

## Note

Pasting into a surface that's a plain shell (not an agent) types the path at the prompt, where pressing Enter tries to execute it and fails with "permission denied" — the file is 0600 and not executable. cmux's own paste behaves the same way. Harmless, but worth knowing.

**The image feature works end-to-end** — that's the one thing I most wanted to prove rather than assume. A real Claude Code session in a cmux surface received a pasted PNG through the new RPC and answered `Magenta — it's a 64×64 image of solid #ff00ff (100% of pixels)`.

Two findings worth your attention:

1. **The transport was broken for this all along.** The bridge's WebSocket read limit was the library default of 32 KiB, and exceeding it doesn't return an error — it closes the connection. Every real photo would have killed the link. Only the live test caught it; every unit test passed happily either way.
2. **cmux has a `terminal.paste_image` RPC, but your installed build doesn't expose it** (`method_not_found` — my clone is newer than the shipped app). So the bridge implements the same mechanism itself, which also makes it version-independent.

Testing across the three PRs: 8 new Go tests, 50 Swift assertions across three suites via `./ios/scripts/run-tests.sh`, plus the live end-to-end run.

The consistent gap remains the iOS UI glue — quick action taps, the pasteboard prompt, the status line. Driving the simulator needs Accessibility permission for the terminal process; grant it and I can close that gap on the next pass.
